Definition: from G150 and κέρδος (gain); sordid:--given to (greedy of) filthy lucre.
BiblicalUsage: Twice, both times as a qualification for church leadership: a deacon must not be greedy of filthy lucre, and a bishop must not be given to filthy lucre. The word joins shame to gain — money got or wanted in a way that disgraces the man who takes it. Paul sets it beside a quick temper, wine, and striking, and holds up blamelessness and a steady life against it.
TheologicalSignificance: A leader who loves money will eventually sell the flock to feed himself. I hold that Paul puts this in the list for a reason: greed is the quiet rot that turns shepherds into hirelings, and the church must watch for it before the damage shows.
